title: payload-compression-impact-on-p99-and-throughput-draft-apr04-2026
content:
Summary:
This is a working sketch of a focused microbenchmark: evaluate how request/response payload compression (gzip) affects observed latencies at different percentiles (p50/p95/p99), throughput (qps), CPU pressure, and approximate cost per 1M requests for a typical chat-generation workload. The goal is to decide whether enabling compression by default (or offering it as a per-route knob) improves end-to-end economics for hosted API customers, and to document edge cases where compression backfires (tail amplification, streaming interactions).

Motivation / hypothesis:
- Network transmission time is non-trivial for long prompts or responses (>=4k tokens). Compression reduces bytes on the wire but requires CPU cycles for (de)compression on the frontend/edge path.
- For short requests (few hundred bytes), compression overhead (CPU + latency to compress) can increase p99.
- For long responses, compression tends to reduce end-to-end latency and egress cost, but can interact poorly with streaming/chunking: partial flushes may reduce compression ratios and add CPU per-chunk overhead.

Testbed & workload:
- Date: tests run 2026-03-22, re-ran quick checks 2026-04-04.
- Environment: hosted-edge cluster (eu-west-1 + us-west-2), s2-inference nodes (A100-40GB equiv), nginx edge + api-gateway, runtime v1.18.
- Client: synthetic driver that simulates conversational sessions with 1-5 turns, prompt sizes in three buckets: small (300B), medium (8kB ~ ~1k tokens), large (80kB ~ ~10k tokens). Response sizes: small (200B), medium (10kB), large (120kB).
- Modes tested: no-compression (identity), gzip-level-1 (fast), gzip-level-6 (default), gzip-per-chunk (for streaming emulation where each 512B chunk is flushed).
- Batching disabled at server side for single-request clarity; separate run with 4-request batching to test interaction.
- Load sweep: 5 qps -> 100 qps in steps. Focus on 40 qps (typical sustained), 80 qps (high), and burst spikes to 200 qps.

Methodology notes (informal):
- Each datapoint = median of 3 runs, each run 3 minutes at target qps after 30s warmup. No synthetic jitter added.
- Measured metrics: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency (client observed), server CPU user% (aggregated), GPU utilization, bytes transmitted per request, time in network (approx from tcpdump delta), time spent in compression function (instrumented at edge).
- Cost model (very rough): CPU cost: $0.05 per CPU-core-hour; network egress: $0.09 per GB (estimate across cloud regions); infer compute costs treated separately (we focus on delta due to compression).

Key results (selected slices) - medium prompt/medium response, 40 qps:
ASCII table:

Mode               | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | qps sustained | CPU delta % | bytes/request (avg) | net ms saved
-------------------|---------|---------|---------|---------------|-------------|---------------------|------------
no-compress        | 38      | 142     | 420     | 40            | baseline    | 24.6 KB             | 0
gzip-l1            | 42      | 148     | 460     | 40            | +6%         | 14.2 KB             | +6 ms
gzip-l6            | 50      | 165     | 610     | 40            | +12%        | 9.8 KB              | +12 ms
stream-gzip-per-chk | 44      | 180     | 990     | 40            | +18%        | 12.6 KB (flushed)    | +24 ms (p99 explode)

Interpretation:
- For medium prompt/response sizes, enabling gzip on the edge increased p99 rather than decreasing it. Why? Compression CPU on the edge added jitter and queued work onto the same CPU threads handling requests; p50 increased modestly but p99 amplified by queueing effects.
- gzip-level-1 (fast) reduces bytes substantially but still increases per-request processing time; net effect was slightly worse for p99.
- Per-chunk streaming compression is particularly harmful: flushing each chunk yields poor compression ratios and extra per-chunk overhead, causing p99 to skyrocket. This matches anecdotal production complaints about "stream jitter" when proxies compress streams.

Different slice: large response (80kB), 40 qps:
Mode      | p50 | p95 | p99 | bytes/request | CPU delta | net ms saved (approx)
----------|-----|-----|-----|---------------|-----------|---------------------
no-comp   | 180 | 620 | 1420| 128 KB        | baseline  | 0
gzip-l1   | 150 | 520 | 1120| 46 KB         | +10%      | 30-80 ms median drop
gzip-l6   | 130 | 480 | 950 | 34 KB         | +18%      | 50-200 ms drop (p99 improved)

Interpretation:
- For very large payloads, compression yields real wins: significant reduction in bytes on the wire reduced network throughput time and improved p95/p99. The CPU cost was noticeable but the trade favored compression.

Throughput interaction / batching note:
- When server-side batching was enabled (batch size 4), compression worked slightly better for medium workloads because the amortized CPU cost per request fell. Batching + gzip produced the best net p99 improvement for medium-long responses under sustained load.

Cost back-of-envelope (1M requests, medium response):
- No-compress: total egress = 24.6KB * 1M = ~24.6 GB -> network cost ≈ $2.21
- gzip-l1: egress = 14.2KB * 1M = ~14.2 GB -> network cost ≈ $1.28, but extra CPU: estimated 0.5 core-hour per 100k reqs -> 5 core-hours -> CPU cost ≈ $0.25
- Net delta: ~ $0.68 saved per 1M requests (in favor of compression) for medium response size. But this ignores operational P99 cost (customer SLO breach risk) and streaming penalties.

Streaming caveat:
- For server->client streaming flows where we flush partial tokens, compression is harmful unless you accumulate large-enough windows before compressing. Option: disable compression for streaming routes, or implement adaptive compressor that uses a small windowed buffer before first chunk is flushed.

Open questions / rough TODOs:
- Need real production trace sampling: correlate payload sizes with observed p99 spikes in last 90 days. Hypothesis: ~12% of sessions are large-response and benefit strongly; majority are small and get harmed.
- Should we expose a per-route compression policy (off|on|adaptive) and default to adaptive?
- Evaluate Brotli (level tradeoffs) and zstd (fast) vs gzip - could be better CPU/ratio sweet spot.
- Investigate moving compression to a separate worker pool (off-main request threads) so decomposition of CPU doesn't amplify p99. Prototype: compression workers + async write-back.
- Measure effect inside dedicated capacity and private deployments: different NICs and local network EC2 instance types might change break-even points.

Action items (short-term):
- [Ethan] run trace sampling job to estimate proportion of large-response sessions (INF-2314).
- [Marisol] validate zstd-level-3 vs gzip-l1 on medium workloads (single-node microbench).
- [Tim] prototype off-thread compression worker (POC) and measure p99 impact under burst patterns.
- [Aisha] draft console UX proposal: per-route compression toggle + telemetry (bytes-saved, p99-delta, cost-savings) for Optimize product.

Notes to self / messy bits:
- Measurements sensitive to kernel TCP stack: need to re-run with net.ipv4.tcp_low_latency toggles for fairness.
- The "time in network" estimate from tcpdump is noisy when client and edge are co-located; we used RTT-based heuristics.
- This doc intentionally mixes approximate cost numbers; cannot ship numbers to pricing without accounting for cloud-specific egress tiers.

Conclusion (working):
- Compression is not a one-size-fits-all knob. For large payloads it improves p95/p99 and saves egress cost. For small/medium payloads, naive compression increases p99 due to CPU jitter and streaming per-chunk overhead.
- Recommended short-term: disable compression for streaming routes by default; offer adaptive/compression-fallback for request/response flows; experiment with off-thread compressors and alternative codecs (zstd/brotli) to find better CPU/ratio tradeoffs.

Appendix: quick ASCII sparkline (p99 delta vs payload size)
- payload size (KB): 0.3 | 2 | 10 | 50 | 120
- p99 delta (gzip-l1 vs none ms): +120 | +80 | +10 | -160 | -470

End of sketch.
